prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize for topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. After round 1 I still think this is the cleanest example on the shortlist of a simple, general mechanism: a Z2 invariant protects edge and surface states against non-magnetic disorder, and it gave condensed-matter physics a new organising principle that is not a broken symmetry. The chain is traceable. Kane and Mele wrote down the Z2 classification and the graphene quantum spin Hall model, and Molenkamp's HgTe quantum wells gave the decisive transport measurement of conductance near 2e^2/h with the expected dependence on gate voltage and device size. About fifteen years of independent transport, ARPES and first-principles work have left the interpretation stable, and the idea has spread to photonics, phononics and cold atoms. A useful result of round 1 is that Eriksson, Olsson and I now name the identical trio, so the dispute inside the committee is no longer about who the three are but about whether three is a fair number. The 2016 prize rewarded topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall topology of bands. It did not reward a time-reversal-invariant topological classification of insulators with protected edge and surface states, so I regard this as a distinct and complementary discovery and not a repetition.
statement.case_against: The credit remains the weak point, and I do not want to hide it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal told Molenkamp which material and which thickness to use, and S.-C. Zhang is deceased, so a prize that follows the experiment omits a decisive theory step. Hasan's 3D spectroscopy of Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 is an independent experimental strand with real consequences for materials, and it is outside the trio. Three members (Kroll, Johansson, Lindroth) and the Chair have said that they cannot place B040 first until the credit is settled, and that is a fair test that I cannot pass perfectly with the three-person cap. I also concede that the optical lattice clock has the cleanest two-name attribution and the broadest support, which makes it the natural fallback and a serious competitor if the committee decides that a flawed but defensible trio is worse than a clean pair.

responses.point: The Chair asks the condensed-matter members to say which two- or three-person set they can all defend, and whether two-dimensional and three-dimensional topological insulators are one achievement.
responses.response: I think they are one achievement. The Z2 invariant that Kane and Mele introduced for the 2D quantum spin Hall state is the same classification that Fu, Kane and Mele extended to 3D, and Hasan's ARPES then tested the 3D prediction on a particular material family. The experiments are two confirmations of one classification, not two discoveries. That is why I would keep the mechanism's two originators and add the first experiment on the effect itself, and why I would drop Hasan before Mele if one name had to go. Since Olsson and Eriksson have both now written the same trio, my answer to your question is that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the set at least three of us can defend with an identical citation, and the committee should treat the omission of BHZ and Hasan as a known cost, written in plainly, not as a hidden flaw.

responses.point: Olsson moved from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp in round 1, on the ground that the two originators of the theory should stay together with the original experiment on the effect itself.
responses.response: I agree with her reasoning and I think her move resolves the disagreement that Pearce, Johansson and Lindroth pointed to, since we no longer propose different trios. Her own caveat is the one I share: the citation has to avoid claiming that the 3D materials work is credited. I would word the part around the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, with the HgTe observation named, so that the 3D spectroscopy and the BHZ proposal are plainly outside the scope of the award and not implied. I also take from her statement that the quantum anomalous Hall effect is a separate, later discovery and should not be bundled in here.

responses.point: Kroll will not support B040 as the preferred configuration on the current record because Mele is excluded by the cap, the HgTe experiment followed BHZ, and Hasan's work is a separate step, whereas the two names for B045 are agreed by every member who ranked it.
responses.response: The attribution argument is correct as far as it goes, and I do not dispute that Katori and Ye is the tidier credit. But a tidy credit is not the same as the stronger discovery. Both of my answers to your point matter. First, the cap does not exclude Mele in my configuration, it excludes Hasan, and I have argued that Hasan's work tests a classification the trio already introduced. Second, the lattice clock inherits the comb and ion-control prizes of 2005 and 2012 and its main consequence, the redefinition of the second, has not happened. I would not object to it as a prize and I accept it as the fallback, but for me it is a sharper version of a measurement paradigm that is already recognised, whereas B040 changed which phases we look for. If the committee judges that a clean credit outweighs that, then I would support B045 over a three-name B040 that members regard as unfair, and I would not hold out.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B016) but says it is premature if the committee wants the source identification confirmed, and that B045 is then the safer, broader alternative.
responses.response: I take his conditional seriously, because it is the same maturity test that I apply to twisted bilayer graphene: whether the central interpretation is settled. By his own account the diffuse flux is settled and the source picture is not, so a citation limited to the diffuse flux is defensible. My difficulty is the one he and Pearce both name, that the Halzen-Karle split against AMANDA-era and other IceCube leaders cannot be settled from the supplied text. I cannot judge that from my field, and I will not put a configuration with a contested pair above one with a stated, bounded credit problem. If the committee shows that the two names are secure, B016 becomes a stronger rival than I allowed in round 1.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a trio that excludes Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, given that Zhang is deceased and the cap is three. This is the question on which my preference depends most.

Whether the 2016 prize makes a topological-insulator citation look repetitive to colleagues who read it as the same story, even though I regard the Z2 classification with protected edge and surface states as distinct.
Whether the Halzen-Karle pair for B016 is secure; I cannot assess the instrument and analysis credit from my own field.

Whether the optical lattice clock should be preferred if the committee decides that attribution clarity should outrank conceptual weight; I regard it as a mature and acceptable alternative, and in that case I would not block it.
statement.conflict_note: No change. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. None of Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, Bistritzer, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero appears among my listed co-authors or institutions. My Gothenburg affiliation is close to Chalmers colleagues on the committee (Johansson, Olsson), but no collaboration with any shortlisted candidate was found, and Johansson's disclosed flag concerns B026 and B008, which are not my preferred configuration.
